articles.body: How to Measure AI Search Visibility in 2026: A Complete Guide Search is changing. Instead of clicking through a list of blue links, users can now ask questions and receive synthesized answers from AI-powered search experiences. Google has AI Overviews and AI Mode, while platforms such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity can surface information from websites as part of their responses. For developers, marketers, and website owners, this creates a new question: How do you know whether your website is actually visible in AI search? Traditional SEO metrics such as rankings, impressions, clicks, and organic traffic are still important. But they don't tell the entire story anymore. A page can rank well in traditional search and still rarely appear as a cited source in AI-generated answers.

articles.body: Late last month a PR opened on our repo: propagating secret taint across workflow steps , a security feature. The numbers: 83 files, 21,962 lines added, 36 commits. And on the way to merge, 209 review conversations across two days. The code was written by Codex. The review was also Codex. What those 209 conversations left behind is what this post is about. Ninety percent of the reviews were accurate Let me be clear about one thing first. Codex reviews PRs well. By my feel, about 90% of its comments are accurate. It catches missed edge cases, drifted semantics, the spots a tired human reviewer would wave through. Before Codex I tried plenty of alternatives: having the main agent review its own work, attaching a different model as a subagent reviewer, running two-stage reviews.

articles.title: Docker BuildKit Cache Setup That Actually Speeds Up CI
articles.excerpt: Originally published on kuryzhev.cloud Last month a client asked me why their "cached" Docker builds still took nine minutes on every single pull request. They had --cache-from in their GitHub Actions…
articles.body: Originally published on kuryzhev.cloud Last month a client asked me why their "cached" Docker builds still took nine minutes on every single pull request. They had --cache-from in their GitHub Actions workflow, a green checkmark, and a nagging suspicion something was off. Turned out their BuildKit cache had never actually hit once in three months — it was pulling a stale :latest tag as cache source and silently falling back to a full rebuild every time. This is the single most common failure mode I see with Docker BuildKit cache CI setups, and it's almost always invisible until someone actually times the build.

articles.body: Rocket Lab plans to start launching even more frequently and flexibly, thanks to a new portable spaceport system called "GHOST." GHOST — short for "Global Hypersonic & Orbital Spaceport Technology" — turns the company's " Electron and HASTE rockets into a launch-anywhere, launch-anytime capability for multi-launch flight campaigns and critical national security missions," Rocket Lab representatives said in a statement today (Aug. 10). "Packaged entirely within standard shipping containers, GHOST deploys complete rockets, launch infrastructure, ground support and range control systems anywhere in the world," they added. Electron is Rocket Lab's workhorse orbital rocket, giving small satellites dedicated rides to the final frontier.
